focus.text: An English sentence needs a subject, a verb and a complete idea. When one of those is missing you have written a fragment; when two sentences are pushed together with nothing between them you have written a run-on; and when a lone comma is doing the joining you have written a comma splice. Punctuation is simply the signal that shows a reader where one idea stops and the next begins. Learn to see the clauses in your own draft and most punctuation problems solve themselves, because the marks follow the joins.

summaryTable.caption: Three sentence faults and how to repair them
rows: Attach it to a main clause: *Few students joined **because the fee was high**.*
The rain started we went inside.
Add a full stop or a conjunction: *The rain started**, so** we went inside.*
Traffic is heavy, many people are late.
Use a full stop, a semicolon or a conjunction: *Traffic is heavy**, so** many people are late.*

pretest.sentence: The library closes at nine, so we finished our revision at home.
pretest.reason: Two independent clauses joined by a comma plus *so* — a correct compound sentence.

pretest.sentence: The bus was late, we missed the first lesson.
pretest.reason: Two full sentences joined by only a comma → comma splice.

pretest.sentence: I stayed at home all weekend. Because the rain never stopped.
pretest.reason: *Because the rain never stopped* is a dependent clause and cannot stand alone.

pretest.sentence: Although the test was long, nobody complained.
pretest.reason: A dependent clause comes first and a comma separates it from the main clause.

pretest.sentence: My uncle drives a lorry he leaves before dawn.
pretest.reason: Two sentences with no punctuation between them → run-on.

pretest.sentence: After the concert finished, the crowd walked down to the river.
pretest.reason: *After…* is a dependent clause in front, so the comma after it is right.

pretest.sentence: There have three markets within a kilometre of my house.
Rents have risen sharply; many young workers now share flats.
pretest.reason: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses.

pretest.sentence: Public transport is improving, however, many people still drive.
pretest.reason: *However* is not a conjunction, so the comma before it leaves a comma splice.

pretest.sentence: We need two things before Friday: a venue and a list of speakers.
pretest.reason: A complete sentence comes before the colon, and the list explains it.

context.title: Mornings on the river
context.paragraph: Cần Thơ is famous for its floating markets, and thousands of visitors come every year. Because the boats set off before sunrise, most tourists book a guide the night before. My aunt has worked on the river since 1998, so she knows which sellers open earliest. She told me that the market is quieter now, although it is still busy at five o'clock. Younger traders have moved to shops on the bank; the rent is higher, but the hours are kinder. When I visited last April, I bought a pineapple from a woman who had sold fruit there for thirty years. She laughed at my question about retirement.

sections.title: Forming clauses and sentences

table.caption: What a clause is and what it can do on its own
rows: subject + verb, opened by a subordinator
The exam finished at four, and we went home.
After the exam finished, we went home.

notes: Subordinators open a dependent clause and stop it standing alone: *because, although, if, unless, when, after, before, while, since, that, who, which*.

options: Because the library was closed on Sunday.
The library was closed on Sunday.
items.reason: *Because…* is a dependent clause and needs a main clause beside it.

items.stem: Choose the sentence that is joined correctly.
options: My sister studies in Huế, my brother works in Đà Nẵng.
My sister studies in Huế, and my brother works in Đà Nẵng.
items.reason: Two independent clauses need a conjunction after the comma.

options: There are two lifts in the building.
There have two lifts in the building.

items.stem: Choose the sentence that is punctuated correctly.
options: We waited an hour the train never came.
We waited an hour, but the train never came.
items.reason: Without a comma and a conjunction the two clauses run on.

options: Walking along the river at sunset.
We walked along the river at sunset.
items.reason: *Walking…* has no subject and no finite verb, so it is a fragment.

sections.title: Using clauses without fragments, run-ons or comma splices

rules.text: A dependent clause must be attached to a main clause; on its own it is a fragment.

examples.text: Few students joined the trip **because the fee was high**.
**Although the rain stopped**, the pitch was still flooded.

rules.text: Two independent clauses cannot be held together by a comma alone. Use a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma plus *and, but, so, or, for, nor, yet*.

examples.text: Traffic is heavy in the morning, **so** many workers leave at six.
Rents keep rising, **and** young workers now share flats.

rules.text: Check that every sentence has a subject and a finite verb; an *-ing* form on its own cannot be the verb.

examples.text: **The team was working** on the poster until midnight.
**Three volunteers arrived** early to move the chairs.

tips: Read your draft aloud and stop at every full stop. If a piece cannot stand on its own as an answer to a question, it is a fragment and belongs to the sentence next to it.

sections.title: Forming sentences with commas, full stops and capitals

table.caption: Where the basic marks go
rows: at the end of a statement
after an introductory word, phrase or clause
before *and, but, so* joining two independent clauses
The fee is small**, but** the queue is long.
between the items of a list
We bought rice, sugar**,** salt and tea.
Ms Hương**, our form teacher,** marked the papers.
first word of a sentence, names, months, nationalities
In **July, Mai** began a course in **Đà Nẵng**.

notes: No comma is needed when the dependent clause comes last: *We left early because the traffic was bad.* The comma is normal when that clause comes first.

items.sentence: The ferry was cancelled, we took the bus instead.
items.reason: Two full sentences joined by only a comma → comma splice.

items.sentence: I could not print my essay. Because the library computers were down.
items.reason: *Because…* is a dependent clause, so it joins the sentence before it.

items.sentence: There have many small cafés around the university.
When the results came out we all met at Hoa's house.
items.reason: A dependent clause in front of the main clause takes a comma after it.

items.sentence: My cousin studies in đà nẵng and comes home every summer.

sections.title: Using semicolons, colons and transitions

rules.text: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.

examples.text: The first survey covered 200 households**;** the second covered 500.
Nobody objected to the plan**;** nobody volunteered for it either.

rules.text: A colon introduces a list or an explanation, and what comes before it must be a complete sentence.

examples.text: The club needs three things**:** a room, a budget and a teacher.
The reason was simple**:** nobody had checked the timetable.

rules.text: Transitions such as *however, therefore, in addition, for example* are not conjunctions. Put a full stop or a semicolon before them and a comma after.

examples.text: Bus fares are low. **However,** the service is slow.
The data came from one city; **therefore,** the results may not apply elsewhere.

rules.text: Say an idea once: *in my opinion* and *I think* do the same job, so choose one of them.

examples.text: **In my opinion,** the school day starts too early.
**I think** the school day starts too early.

notes: *Fares are low, however, the service is slow.* is still a comma splice. A transition never does the work of *but*.
tips: A semicolon is only worth using when the two ideas clearly belong together. If you cannot explain the link in a word, a full stop is the better mark.

model: The first survey covered 200 households; the second covered 500.
items.focus: semicolon between two closely linked clauses
items.reason: The two clauses are the same idea measured twice, so a semicolon shows the link without a conjunction.

sentences: Fares on the new line are low.
model: Fares on the new line are low. However, the service is still slow.
Fares on the new line are low; however, the service is still slow.
items.focus: transition after a full stop or a semicolon
items.reason: *However* is not a conjunction, so a full stop or a semicolon must come before it.

sentences: It needs a room, a budget and a teacher.
model: The club needs three things: a room, a budget and a teacher.
items.reason: A complete sentence comes before the colon, and the list explains it.

model: Because the fee was high, few students joined the course.
The fee was high, so few students joined the course.
items.focus: cause and result in one sentence
items.reason: *Because* turns the first idea into a dependent clause, which then takes a comma before the main clause.

sentences: I waited at the stop for an hour.
model: I waited at the stop for an hour, but the bus never came.
items.focus: comma plus conjunction instead of a comma splice
items.reason: A comma on its own would be a comma splice, so *but* has to follow it.

editing.text: Last term our school started a recycling project, at first only ten students joined. We collected cardboard boxes from the market. Because we had no money for proper bins. There have three classrooms on the ground floor, and the boxes fitted neatly beside the doors. our teacher photographed the first collection and put the picture on the noticeboard. In my opinion, I think the picture did more than any announcement. Numbers grew quickly by December almost sixty students were helping. We now sort three kinds of waste paper, plastic and metal. The project is not perfect, however, it has changed how people in the school think about rubbish. If the council collects our paper every month we will be able to buy proper bins next year.

errors.reason: Two full sentences joined by only a comma → comma splice.
*Because…* is a dependent clause, so it joins the sentence before it.
The first word of a sentence takes a capital letter.
*In my opinion* and *I think* say the same thing; keep one of them.
Two sentences with no punctuation between them → run-on.

errors.span: three kinds of waste paper, plastic and metal
errors.fix: three kinds of waste: paper, plastic and metal
errors.reason: A colon introduces the list that explains *three kinds of waste*.
*However* is not a conjunction, so a semicolon or a full stop must come before it.
A dependent clause in front of the main clause takes a comma after it.

topics.prompt: Write an email to your head teacher proposing a new after-school club. Explain what it would do, who would run it and what it would need.
checklist: Every sentence has a subject and a finite verb, so there are no fragments.
Two independent clauses are never joined by a comma alone.
A comma follows every introductory phrase or dependent clause.

topics.prompt: "Secondary schools should teach cooking and budgeting as ordinary subjects." Give your opinion with two reasons and one example.
checklist: At least one semicolon correctly joins two closely related clauses.
Transitions such as *however* and *therefore* follow a full stop or a semicolon, with a comma after them.
*In my opinion* and *I think* never appear in the same sentence.

topics.prompt: Describe the busiest street near your home at two different times of day: early morning and late evening.
checklist: The paragraph mixes simple, compound and complex sentences.
Clauses beginning with *when, because* or *although* are attached to a main clause.
Lists are separated by commas, and a colon introduces a list only after a complete sentence.
